tips.title: Never change a subscript
tips.body: A subscript is part of the **identity of the substance**. Turning H₂O into H₂O₂ balances an equation for a reaction that does not happen. Only the **big numbers in front** may change — they say *how many*, not *what*.

tips.title: Expand brackets before adding
tips.body: Mg(OH)₂ is $24 + 2(16+1) = 58$, **not** $24 + 16 + 1 = 41$. The subscript multiplies **everything** inside. Writing the expansion out costs a second and saves the mark.

tips.title: The mass check is free
tips.body: If the atoms balance, the relative formula masses must too. CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ gives $100 = 56 + 44$. It catches an error **without your knowing the right answer**, which is the best kind of check.

tips.title: Atoms counted is not mass shared
tips.body: Water has **twice as many hydrogen atoms** as oxygen and is nearly **89% oxygen by mass**, because one oxygen atom is sixteen times heavier. Questions are set to catch this exact assumption.

tips.title: Leave oxygen until last
tips.body: Balance the element that appears in the **fewest places** first. Hydrogen and oxygen usually turn up everywhere, and they often come right on their own once the rest is done.

why.matters:
A formula is a claim about exactly which atoms are in a substance; a balanced equation is a claim that none of them went missing on the way. Together they are what makes chemistry quantitative — they let you say, before touching anything, how much oxygen a reaction will need and how much product it could possibly give.

Balancing is not a puzzle invented by examiners. It is **conservation of mass written down**. Every atom that goes in comes out again attached to something else, and the numbers in front are the bookkeeping that proves it.

examples.title: Why a litre of petrol makes 2.3 kg of carbon dioxide
examples.body:
A litre of petrol weighs about three quarters of a kilogram, and burning it sends about **2.3 kg** of carbon dioxide out of the exhaust. That reads like a mistake until you count atoms: the extra mass is **oxygen taken from the air**, not from the tank.

Petrol is close enough to octane: $\mathrm{2C_8H_{18} + 25O_2 \rightarrow 16CO_2 + 18H_2O}$. For every 1 kg of fuel the engine pulls in about 3.5 kg of oxygen, and 4.5 kg comes out — 3.1 kg of carbon dioxide and 1.4 kg of water.

props.caption: Nothing is created: the extra mass came out of the air

visual.alt: Three bars in proportion: one kilogram of petrol going in, three and a half kilograms of oxygen drawn from the air, and four and a half kilograms of gas leaving the exhaust

examples.title: Why hydrogen peroxide is not water
examples.body:
Hydrogen peroxide has one more oxygen atom per molecule than water does. It bleaches hair, it fizzes on a cut, it slowly falls apart into water and oxygen, and you would not drink it.

So a subscript can never be adjusted to make an equation balance. $\mathrm{H_2 + O_2 \rightarrow H_2O_2}$ balances perfectly and describes a reaction that does not happen; $\mathrm{2H_2 + O_2 \rightarrow 2H_2O}$ is the one that does. The big numbers in front say **how many**. The little ones say **what the substance is**, and changing those changes the chemical.

visual.alt: A table setting water against hydrogen peroxide: the same two elements, relative formula masses of eighteen against thirty-four, one of them drinking water and the other a bleach, separated only by a subscript

examples.title: Why a cement works sends nearly half its rock up the chimney
examples.body:
Cement starts as limestone, and the first step is to roast it: $\mathrm{CaCO_3 \rightarrow CaO + CO_2}$. Put the masses in and the problem is unavoidable. 100 kg of limestone gives 56 kg of quicklime and 44 kg of carbon dioxide.

Those 44 kg are not waste from a badly run kiln — they are the equation. Every tonne of quicklime releases about **0.79 tonnes** of carbon dioxide before a single shovel of fuel is burned, and no amount of efficiency can change the ratio.

props.caption: 44 kg of every 100 leaves as gas, by the equation alone

visual.alt: Three bars in proportion showing one hundred kilograms of limestone roasting into fifty-six kilograms of quicklime and forty-four kilograms of carbon dioxide that goes up the chimney

steps.title: Conservation of mass
steps.body:
**The law of conservation of mass states that no atoms are lost or made during a chemical reaction, so the mass of the products equals the mass of the reactants.**

That is the sentence to learn, and the reason follows directly from what a chemical reaction is: atoms are **rearranged**, not created or destroyed. The same atoms that went in come out, joined differently.

**This is why equations must balance.** If no atoms are lost or made, then every element must have the **same number of atoms on both sides** of the equation. A symbol equation that does not balance is claiming atoms appeared or vanished, which cannot happen.

**So balancing is not a ritual.** It is the equation being made to tell the truth about the atoms.

**An example.** Heating calcium carbonate:

$$\mathrm{CaCO_3 \rightarrow CaO + CO_2}$$

Count the atoms: one calcium, one carbon and three oxygens on the left; one calcium, one carbon, and one plus two equals three oxygens on the right. Balanced.

**And because the atoms balance, the masses must too.** The relative formula mass of $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ is 100; of $\mathrm{CaO}$ it is 56 and of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ it is 44. And $56 + 44 = 100$. That is not a coincidence — it is conservation of mass showing up in the arithmetic, and it gives you a free check on any balanced equation.

steps.title: The two kinds of number
steps.body:
Equations contain **two** kinds of number, and they do completely different jobs. Confusing them is the commonest error in this topic.

**A big number in front of a formula** — a **multiplier**, written in normal script — multiplies **the whole formula**.

**A small number inside a formula** — a **subscript** — multiplies **only the atom it follows**.

$$2\mathrm{H_2O} \quad \text{means} \quad \textbf{two} \text{ water molecules}$$

In $2\mathrm{H_2O}$ there are **4 hydrogen atoms** and **2 oxygen atoms**: the subscript 2 gives two hydrogens per molecule, and the multiplier 2 doubles everything.

**Worked through:**

| Written | Hydrogen atoms | Oxygen atoms |
|---|---|---|
| $\mathrm{H_2O}$ | 2 | 1 |
| $2\mathrm{H_2O}$ | 4 | 2 |
| $3\mathrm{H_2O}$ | 6 | 3 |

**The rule that matters most:** when balancing, you may **only** change the **big numbers in front**. You may **never** change a subscript.

Changing a subscript changes the **substance**. $\mathrm{H_2O}$ is water; $\mathrm{H_2O_2}$ is hydrogen peroxide, which is a different chemical with different properties. Balancing an equation by turning water into hydrogen peroxide gets a balanced equation that describes a reaction which does not happen.

**Brackets** work the same way as a multiplier, but inside a formula. $\mathrm{Mg(OH)_2}$ has one magnesium, **two** oxygens and **two** hydrogens — the subscript 2 applies to everything in the brackets.

steps.title: Balancing an equation
steps.body:
Balancing is **counting, then adjusting the big numbers, then counting again**. Work through one element at a time and leave the ones that appear in several places until last.

The first example below balances in one move. The second is the kind the exam actually sets: **oxygen appears in both products**, so its total cannot be known until carbon and hydrogen are settled — which is what *leave it until last* means in practice.

steps.title: Relative formula mass
steps.body:
**The relative formula mass, $M_r$, of a compound is the sum of the relative atomic masses of the atoms in the numbers shown in the formula.**

So you add up the relative atomic masses, counting each atom as many times as the formula says.

**Worked through:**

- $\mathrm{H_2O}$: two hydrogens and one oxygen $= (2 \times 1) + 16 = 18$
- $\mathrm{CO_2}$: one carbon and two oxygens $= 12 + (2 \times 16) = 44$
- $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$: $40 + 12 + (3 \times 16) = 100$
- $\mathrm{Mg(OH)_2}$: the subscript applies to everything in the brackets, so $24 + 2 \times (16 + 1) = 24 + 34 = 58$

**Brackets are where the marks go.** $\mathrm{Mg(OH)_2}$ is **not** $24 + 16 + 1 = 41$. The 2 multiplies **both** the oxygen and the hydrogen. Expand the brackets before adding anything.

**And the second half of the spec point:**

> **In a balanced chemical equation, the sum of the relative formula masses of the reactants in the quantities shown equals the sum for the products in the quantities shown.**

That is conservation of mass again, and it is a **free check**. For $\mathrm{CaCO_3 \rightarrow CaO + CO_2}$:

- reactants: $100$
- products: $56 + 44 = 100$

If those two totals do not match, either the equation is not balanced or an $M_r$ is wrong — and you know to look before you go further.

steps.title: Percentage by mass
steps.body:
You should be able to **calculate the percentage by mass of an element in a compound**, given the relative formula mass and the relative atomic masses.

$$\% \text{ by mass} = \frac{A_r \times \text{number of that atom}}{M_r} \times 100$$

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
**Part A.**

1. State the law of conservation of mass.
2. How many atoms of each element are there in $2\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$?
3. Explain the difference between the 2 in $2\mathrm{H_2O}$ and the 2 in $\mathrm{H_2O}$.

**Part B.** Relative atomic masses: H 1, C 12, N 14, O 16, Na 23, Mg 24, S 32, Cl 35.5, Ca 40.

4. Calculate the $M_r$ of $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$.
5. Calculate the $M_r$ of $\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2}$.
6. Calculate the percentage by mass of nitrogen in $\mathrm{NH_3}$.

**Part C.**

7. Balance: $\mathrm{Na + Cl_2 \rightarrow NaCl}$
8. Balance: $\mathrm{CH_4 + O_2 \rightarrow CO_2 + H_2O}$
9. A student balances $\mathrm{H_2 + O_2 \rightarrow H_2O}$ by changing the product to $\mathrm{H_2O_2}$. Explain why this is wrong, and balance it properly.

For question 5, expand the brackets before you add anything.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Balancing is conservation of mass, not a puzzle.** Atoms are rearranged, never created or destroyed, so every element must appear the same number of times on both sides. Saying that in an answer — rather than just producing balanced numbers — is what a question asking *why must equations be balanced?* is looking for.

**Never change a subscript.** This is the rule, and the reason is what matters: a subscript is part of the **identity of the substance**. Turning $\mathrm{H_2O}$ into $\mathrm{H_2O_2}$ to make the numbers work produces a balanced equation for a reaction that does not happen — water and hydrogen peroxide are different chemicals. Only the **multipliers in front** may change, because they say *how many*, not *what*.

**The mass check is free, and it is independent.** If the atoms balance, the relative formula masses must balance too. So totalling the $M_r$ on each side catches an error you might otherwise carry forward, and it catches it **without knowing the right answer** — which is the most valuable kind of check there is.

**Expand brackets before adding.** $\mathrm{Mg(OH)_2}$ is $24 + 2(16 + 1) = 58$, not $24 + 16 + 1 = 41$. The subscript multiplies **everything** inside. This single slip accounts for a large share of the lost marks in $M_r$ questions, and it is entirely avoidable by writing the expansion out.

**Number of atoms is not share of mass.** Water has **twice as many hydrogen atoms as oxygen atoms** and is nearly **89% oxygen by mass**, because one oxygen atom is sixteen times heavier than one hydrogen atom. Questions are set precisely to catch the assumption that the commonest atom contributes the most mass.

**Start with the element that appears in the fewest places.** Balancing is easier from the outside in: deal with elements that appear in one compound on each side first, and leave hydrogen and oxygen until last, since they usually turn up everywhere. Often they come right on their own, as the magnesium and hydrochloric acid example shows.

**And when a reaction seems to lose or gain mass**, the explanation is almost always a **gas**. A metal burning gains mass because oxygen from the air has joined it; a carbonate decomposing loses mass because carbon dioxide has escaped. Conservation of mass is not broken — something left, or arrived, without being weighed.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Law of conservation of mass**: no atoms are **lost or made** in a chemical reaction, so the **mass of the products equals the mass of the reactants**.
- Atoms are **rearranged**, not created or destroyed — which is **why equations must balance**.
- A **big number in front** is a **multiplier**: it multiplies the **whole formula**.
- A **small number inside** is a **subscript**: it multiplies **only the atom before it**.
- $2\mathrm{H_2O}$ has **4 hydrogens** and **2 oxygens**.
- When balancing, change **only the big numbers in front**. **Never change a subscript** — that changes the substance.
- Balance one element at a time, starting with the one that appears in the **fewest places**.
- **Brackets**: the subscript applies to **everything inside**. $\mathrm{Mg(OH)_2}$ has two O and two H.
- **Relative formula mass $M_r$** is the **sum of the relative atomic masses of the atoms in the numbers shown in the formula**.
- $\mathrm{H_2O} = 18$, $\mathrm{CO_2} = 44$, $\mathrm{CaCO_3} = 100$, $\mathrm{Mg(OH)_2} = 58$.
- In a balanced equation the **total $M_r$ of the reactants equals the total for the products** — a **free check**.
- **Percentage by mass** $= \dfrac{A_r \times \text{number of atoms}}{M_r} \times 100$.
- **Number of atoms is not share of mass**: water is nearly **89% oxygen** with twice as many hydrogen atoms.
- An apparent **gain or loss of mass** means a **gas** joined or escaped.

questions.prompt: Explain why chemical equations must be balanced, and describe how to balance one. Use Mg + HCl to MgCl2 + H2 as your example.
questions.solution: Chemical equations must be balanced because of the law of conservation of mass, which states that no atoms are lost or made during a chemical reaction, so the mass of the products equals the mass of the reactants. In a reaction the atoms present are simply rearranged into new combinations, so every element must appear the same number of times on both sides of the equation. An equation that does not balance is claiming that atoms have appeared or disappeared, which cannot happen. To balance an equation, first count the atoms of each element on each side. For magnesium reacting with hydrochloric acid the left hand side has one magnesium, one hydrogen and one chlorine, and the right hand side has one magnesium, two chlorines and two hydrogens. Magnesium is already balanced with one atom on each side, so it can be left alone. Chlorine is not balanced, since there is one on the left and two on the right, so a two is placed in front of HCl. Because this is a multiplier it doubles the whole formula, giving two hydrogen atoms and two chlorine atoms on the left. Recounting shows one magnesium, two hydrogens and two chlorines on each side, so the equation is now balanced and reads Mg plus 2HCl gives MgCl2 plus H2. Only the large number in front was changed. It is essential never to change a subscript, because a subscript is part of the identity of the substance and altering it would describe a different chemical altogether. Finally the answer can be checked by totalling the relative formula masses, which give ninety seven on each side.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Why equations balance.** The **law of conservation of mass**: no atoms are lost or made in a reaction, so the mass of the products equals the mass of the reactants. Atoms are **rearranged**, not created or destroyed — so every element must appear the **same number of times on both sides**. An unbalanced equation claims atoms appeared or vanished.

**Balancing the example:**

1. **Count.** Left: 1 Mg, 1 H, 1 Cl. Right: 1 Mg, 2 Cl, 2 H.
2. **Magnesium is already balanced** — one each side, so leave it.
3. **Chlorine is not** — 1 against 2. Put a **2 in front of HCl**.
4. That is a **multiplier**, so it doubles the whole formula: now 2 H and 2 Cl on the left.
5. **Recount.** 1 Mg, 2 H, 2 Cl on each side.

$$\mathrm{Mg + 2HCl \rightarrow MgCl_2 + H_2}$$

**Only the big number in front changed.** Never change a **subscript** — it is part of the **identity of the substance**, and altering it describes a different chemical.

**The free check:** total the relative formula masses. $24 + 2(36.5) = 97$ on the left; $95 + 2 = 97$ on the right.

questions.prompt: Water contains twice as many hydrogen atoms as oxygen atoms, yet it is almost 89% oxygen by mass. Explain this, and explain how percentage by mass is calculated.
questions.solution: The apparent contradiction comes from confusing the number of atoms with the share of the mass, which are two different things. A water molecule contains two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom, so by number the hydrogen atoms outnumber the oxygen atoms two to one. However, the atoms do not weigh the same. The relative atomic mass of hydrogen is one and that of oxygen is sixteen, so a single oxygen atom has sixteen times the mass of a single hydrogen atom. The two hydrogen atoms together contribute only two units of relative mass, while the one oxygen atom contributes sixteen, so oxygen accounts for the great majority of the mass despite being outnumbered. Percentage by mass is calculated by taking the total relative mass contributed by the element in question, which is its relative atomic mass multiplied by the number of atoms of it in the formula, dividing that by the relative formula mass of the whole compound, and multiplying by one hundred. For water the relative formula mass is two times one plus sixteen, which is eighteen. The oxygen contributes sixteen of those eighteen units, so the percentage by mass of oxygen is sixteen divided by eighteen multiplied by one hundred, which is 88.9 per cent to one decimal place. The remaining 11.1 per cent is hydrogen, and the two percentages add to one hundred, which is a useful check on any answer of this kind.

states that an oxygen atom has sixteen times the mass of a hydrogen atom

calculates the Mr of water as 18 and the percentage as about 88.9

criteria.text: Separates atom count from mass share

questions.modelAnswer:
**The confusion** is between the **number of atoms** and the **share of the mass** — two different things.

A water molecule has **two hydrogens and one oxygen**, so hydrogen outnumbers oxygen two to one. But the atoms do not weigh the same: $A_r(\mathrm{H}) = 1$ and $A_r(\mathrm{O}) = 16$, so **one oxygen atom is sixteen times heavier than one hydrogen atom**.

The two hydrogens contribute **2** units of relative mass; the single oxygen contributes **16**. So oxygen dominates the mass despite being outnumbered.

**The calculation:**

$$\% \text{ by mass} = \frac{A_r \times \text{number of atoms}}{M_r} \times 100$$

For water, $M_r = (2 \times 1) + 16 = 18$, so oxygen is

$$\frac{16}{18} \times 100 = 88.9\%$$

**The check worth doing:** the remaining **11.1%** is hydrogen, and the percentages of all the elements in a compound **add to 100**.

examTechnique.body:
State conservation of mass in full when asked why equations balance: no atoms are lost or made, so the masses are equal.

Change only the numbers in front of formulae, never a subscript.

Count the atoms of each element on both sides before and after balancing.

Start with the element that appears in the fewest places and leave oxygen until last.

Expand brackets before adding relative atomic masses.

Check a balanced equation by totalling the relative formula masses on each side.

For percentage by mass, divide the mass contributed by that element by the relative formula mass of the whole compound.

Explain an apparent change in mass by a gas escaping or joining.
examinerErrors: Changing a subscript to balance an equation.
Reading Mg(OH)2 as 24 + 16 + 1 instead of expanding the brackets.
Assuming the element with the most atoms contributes the most mass.
Saying conservation of mass is broken when a reaction appears to gain or lose mass.
Dividing by the relative atomic mass instead of the relative formula mass.
Forgetting that a multiplier applies to every atom in the formula it precedes.
Giving the law of conservation of mass without saying that no atoms are lost or made.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer treats balancing as conservation of mass rather than as arithmetic, and can say why a subscript must never change: it is part of the substance's identity, so altering it describes a different chemical. It expands brackets before adding, totals the relative formula masses on both sides as a free and independent check, and never assumes that the commonest atom contributes the most mass. When a reaction appears to gain or lose mass it looks for the gas rather than doubting the law.
